title: Model risk management for AI systems: what the guidance says and does not say
summary: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. The United States banking agencies' revised model risk guidance (SR-26-2, April 2026) describes a programme of development, validation and governance built around a model inventory and independent 'effective challenge', and it says in its own footnote that generative AI and agentic AI models are not within its scope. This lesson reads that guidance and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework together: what each defines, which principles an engineering team can carry over to LLM and agent systems as practice rather than requirement, and how to tier systems so that the controls match the exposure.

subtopics.title: What model risk is, and the three parts of a programme

blocks.text: The banking agencies define a model narrowly. The revised guidance calls a model "a complex quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, or financial theories to process input data into quantitative estimates", and it says the term "excludes simple arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets, as well as deterministic rule-based processes and software where there are no statistical, economic, or financial theories underpinning their design or use". The earlier text was wider: a method that applies "statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques, and assumptions", built from an input component, a processing component and a reporting component. A trained classifier fits both definitions. A lookup table or a hard-coded rule engine fits neither.

Model risk is defined by its consequences, not by the technology. The earlier guidance called it "the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports", and it named two causes: a model may have fundamental errors and produce inaccurate outputs, or it may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. The revised text keeps the idea and narrows the harm to "the potential for adverse financial consequences associated with models, which may result from decisions made based on model output". It adds a sentence worth keeping on a wall: "even a fundamentally sound model producing accurate outputs consistent with the model's design objective can exhibit high model risk if it is misapplied or misused".

blocks.caption: The three parts of a model risk programme, as the two texts name them
rows: IV. Model Development, Implementation, and Use
IV. Model Development and Model Use
Purpose, design, data, testing before use, documented limitations, and the discipline of using a model only for what it was built for
Independent review of conceptual soundness, analysis of outcomes against reality, and monitoring once the model is in use
Board and senior management roles, policies, the model inventory, documentation, and internal audit's review of the whole

blocks.text: The revised guidance also gives the vocabulary that drives everything else in this lesson. Model risk "is influenced by a model's inherent risk, exposure, purpose, and use". Inherent risk comes from the model itself: its assumptions, its complexity, the quality of its inputs. Exposure is "the significance of the model output to a banking organization's business decisions". Purpose is what the output is used for, with regulatory and financial-risk uses counted as greater risk. "Model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality", and rigour should be "commensurate with" the risk: models deemed immaterial may need only identification and monitoring of the conditions under which they could become material, while material ones warrant more. That is a tiering rule in all but name, and the last subtopic turns it into one.

Model risk is about decisions, not code. A perfect model used for the wrong decision carries model risk; a crude model whose output nobody acts on carries almost none. Start every assessment from the decision the output feeds.

subtopics.title: SR-26-2: what it is, what it replaced, and who it is for

blocks.text: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which call themselves "the agencies", issued the revised Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management jointly. The Federal Reserve published it as SR letter 26-2 and the OCC as Bulletin 2026-13, each with the guidance attached. It is supervisory guidance, and the text says so in its first section: "This guidance does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements; accordingly, non-compliance with this guidance will not result in supervisory criticism against a banking organization." The OCC's news release makes the same point. Everything this lesson draws from it is therefore a description of sound practice, not a rule that binds anyone.

blocks.text: Why does a lesson for engineers who may never work in a bank care about this document? Because it is the most complete public description of a model risk programme that has been exercised for fifteen years. The letter says the revision "reflects supervisory experience and industry feedback accumulated over the past fifteen years", and the OCC bulletin says its purpose is to "clarify model risk management principles" and "set forth a risk-based approach" tailored "to a banking organization's model risk profile and the size and complexity of its operations". When a customer's risk team asks how your system is validated, inventoried and monitored, they are asking in this vocabulary whether or not they cite the letter.

What changed in shape between the two texts is visible from the headings alone. The old guidance addressed "banks"; the new one addresses "banking organizations" and keeps saying that practices appropriate for one organisation "may be inappropriate and ineffective" for another with a different risk profile or purpose. The definition of a model gained the word "complex" and an explicit carve-out for deterministic software. Validation and monitoring now share a section. And the scope statement about generative and agentic AI, which the next subtopic quotes in full, is new: the earlier text never mentioned either.

Cite the guidance by letter and date and quote it rather than paraphrase. The active Federal Reserve letter list no longer carries the superseded letter, and the old letter's page now returns not-found; only its attachment PDF is still served. Links to superseded guidance rot.

subtopics.title: Scope: what is in, what is out, and the footnote on generative and agentic AI

blocks.text: Two sentences set the scope. The definition of a model, quoted in the first subtopic, keeps spreadsheets and rule engines out. The third footnote keeps the newest systems out, and it is short enough to read whole:

Footnote 3 of the revised guidance: "Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance. Nonetheless, a banking organization's risk management and governance practices should guide the determination of appropriate governance and controls for any tools, processes, or systems not covered in this document. However, the principles described in this guidance apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and non-generative, non-agentic AI models."

Read it for what it says and for what it does not. It says the guidance applies to traditional statistical models and to "non-generative, non-agentic AI models": a gradient-boosted fraud score or a logistic credit scorecard is in. It says generative and agentic models are not within scope, which is a statement about the document, not about the systems: it does not say they are unregulated, safe, or exempt from a bank's own governance. It sends them back to "a banking organization's risk management and governance practices", which is why this lesson keeps saying practice, not requirement. And it gives no definition of "generative" or "agentic", so the line between a non-generative AI model and a generative one is yours to draw and document. The OCC bulletin adds that the agencies plan a request for information on exactly this use of AI, so the gap is acknowledged, not accidental.

Nothing stops you from applying the same principles to the out-of-scope systems; this lesson's position is that you should, and label it as practice.

blocks.text: Do not write "our LLM system complies with SR-26-2" in a design document or a customer questionnaire. The guidance says such systems are not within its scope, so the sentence is wrong on its face, and a reader who knows the footnote will stop trusting the rest of the page. Write that the system is governed under the organisation's model risk practices, informed by the guidance's principles and by NIST AI RMF.

subtopics.title: What carries over to LLM and agent systems as practice: inventory, effective challenge, validation, monitoring

blocks.text: Everything in this subtopic is practice, not requirement: the footnote hands generative and agentic systems to the organisation's own practices, and these are the ones worth adopting. The reason is not deference to a regulator. Each principle below was designed for a system whose behaviour cannot be fully read from its code, whose inputs drift, and whose output feeds decisions made by people who did not build it. That describes a language model system at least as well as it describes a credit scorecard.

nodes.label: Model inventory: purpose, status, materiality, owner, validation dates
Independent validation: conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis
Effective challenge: expertise, independence, standing to effect change
Ongoing monitoring: inputs, outputs, outcomes, changes

edges.label: development evidence: design, data, tests, limitations
approved for use (or use under limits)
evaluates whether the practices are rigorous and effective

steps.caption: The owner registers the model before it is built, so the inventory holds models "under development or in use", not only live ones.
Development evidence goes to a validator who did not build the model: what it is for, what data trained it, what tests it passed, where it is known to be weak.
Effective challenge is the critical analysis by people with the expertise, independence and organisational standing to force a change; it is a role, not a meeting.
Validation returns findings and conditions; recommendations, responses and exceptions are tracked in writing.
Validation generally happens before first use; if urgent need forces earlier use, limits and closer monitoring stand in.
In use, the model's outputs and the decisions made on them flow to monitoring, together with the real outcomes they predicted.
Monitoring that shows deterioration, drift or a changed environment sends the model back for revalidation.
Status changes (in use, limited, retired) and findings go back into the inventory, which otherwise rots.
Internal audit reviews the programme itself: are validations independent, is the inventory complete, are findings closed.

subtopics.title: Vendor and third-party models: what you can and cannot validate

blocks.text: Most LLM systems are built on a model someone else trained and often hosts. The guidance has a section for that situation, and its first admission is the useful one: a banking organisation "may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or methodology". It does not treat that as an excuse. "Nevertheless, the principles of model risk management remain applicable", and sound practice "includes developing an understanding of the vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance". Validation of vendor products is done "either by internal or outside parties", ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis still apply, and where a vendor model is customised, sound practice involves "documenting, justifying, and evaluating" the adjustments as part of validation.

The 2011 text was more specific about what to ask for. "Vendors should provide appropriate testing results that show their product works as expected", should "clearly indicate the model's limitations and assumptions and where the product's use may be problematic", and should be expected to run their own ongoing monitoring with disclosure to clients. Then the sentence that matters most for a hosted foundation model: "Banks are expected to validate their own use of vendor products." And because vendors change and disappear, "Banks should have contingency plans for instances when the vendor model is no longer available or cannot be supported by the vendor."

blocks.caption: What you can validate when the model is yours versus vendor-hosted
rows: Known; documented in the development evidence
Record what the vendor publishes about data and cut-off; treat the rest as an unknown in the validation report
Validate behaviour, not internals: your prompts, your retrieval, your tools, your test set
Design review of the method against the purpose
Design review of your use of the model: why this model, this prompt, this grounding
The vendor's documentation is evidence about the model; your design document is evidence about the use
Possible in full for your use case
Graded samples from production, repeated after every vendor version change
Yours for your traffic; the vendor's for the model
Pin versions where the vendor allows it; log the model identifier with every call
Vendor may retire or change the model
A second model behind the same evaluation gate, and a documented fallback

blocks.text: NIST says the same thing in its own structure. GOVERN 6 of the AI RMF covers third-party software and data: 6.1 asks for policies to address AI risks arising from third-party entities and 6.2 for contingency processes for failures in third-party data or AI systems. The Generative AI Profile names "Value Chain and Component Integration" as a risk in its own right, describing "non-transparent or untraceable integration of upstream third-party components" and improper supplier vetting, and its MANAGE 3.1 action lists the controls an organisation applies on top of a third-party model: "filtering GAI input and outputs, grounding, fine tuning, retrieval-augmented generation". Those are engineering controls, and they belong in the validation report as the part of the system that is yours to defend.

A vendor's model card or system card is evidence about the model. It is not evidence about your use of it. A validator who files the vendor's benchmark table as the outcomes analysis for your customer chatbot has validated nothing; the profile's MS-2.5-001 warns against extrapolating performance "from narrow, non-systematic, and anecdotal assessments".

subtopics.title: Where NIST AI RMF 1.0 and the Generative AI Profile fill the gap

blocks.text: The banking guidance tells you how to run a programme; it does not list the risks peculiar to AI, and for generative and agentic systems it steps aside. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework was written for that space. Version 1.0 was released on January 26, 2023 and describes itself as "voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic". Its Core has four functions, GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, each broken into categories and subcategories, and it says of them: "Actions do not constitute a checklist, nor are they necessarily an ordered set of steps." Governance is "a cross-cutting function to inform and be infused throughout the other three functions".

blocks.caption: AI RMF functions and the subcategories that line up with the model risk programme
columns: Subcategories that map to model risk practice
rows: 1.5 ongoing monitoring and periodic review; 1.6 inventory of AI systems; 1.7 decommissioning; 6 third-party software and data; and the accountability category for roles and responsibilities
1.5 organisational risk tolerances "determined and documented"; impact assessment of each identified use
"employs quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools"; systems "should be tested before their deployment and regularly while in operation"
2.5 valid and reliable, with limits of generalisability documented; 2.7 security and resilience evaluated
Allocates resources "to mapped and measured risks"
3.1 third-party risks monitored and controls documented; 4.1 post-deployment monitoring plans including appeal, override, decommissioning, incident response

blocks.text: The Generative AI Profile was released in July 2024 as "a cross-sectoral profile of and companion resource for the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) for Generative AI". A profile, in the framework's own terms, is an implementation of the functions for a specific setting. This one does two things the banking guidance does not. It names a set of risks "unique to or exacerbated by" generative AI, twelve of them, from CBRN information through confabulation ("the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content"), data privacy, harmful bias, human-AI configuration (automation bias and over-reliance), information security, to value chain and component integration. And it attaches suggested actions to the framework's subcategories, each with an identifier, so that a validation plan can point at them. GV-1.3-001, for instance, lists the factors to weigh when defining risk tiers for generative AI; the tiering subtopic uses it.

Two things to know before you lean on it. First, the profile does not use the word "agentic"; the phrase "autonomous agents" appears once, in MEASURE 2.7, as a threat to assess under security and resilience. For agents you have the framework's general functions and your own judgement. Second, both documents are moving. As read for this lesson (dates in the sources list), the NIST framework page says "The AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan", and the Playbook page says the Playbook "will be updated after the AI RMF is revised". Cite the version and date you used, and expect subcategory numbers to change.

Use the two sources for what each is good at. Take the programme vocabulary from the banking guidance: inventory, effective challenge, validation before use, outcomes analysis, monitoring, documentation. Take the AI-specific risk list and the per-subcategory actions from the AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile. Map one onto the other in your policy once, so every validation report follows the same outline.

subtopics.title: Tiering systems by risk: questions, tiers, controls

blocks.text: Both sources hand you the ingredients of a tiering scheme without naming tiers. The banking guidance says rigour should be commensurate with risk, defines materiality as purpose together with exposure, weighs inherent risk against it, and says models deemed immaterial may need only identification and monitoring. The AI RMF asks in MAP 1.5 that risk tolerances be "determined and documented", and the Generative AI Profile's GV-1.3-001 lists factors for risk tiers, among them: impacts to information integrity, dependencies on other systems, harm to fundamental rights or public safety, obscene, discriminatory, invalid or untruthful output, psychological impacts to humans such as anthropomorphization and emotional entanglement, possibility of malicious use, new security vulnerabilities, uneven impact across groups, and variability of performance over time. A tier is just a documented answer to those questions that maps onto a fixed set of controls.

This lesson's tier rule, stated so the worked example can be checked: ask three questions in order. Does the output decide or act on money, people or legal standing without a person approving each case? If yes, the system is high tier. Otherwise, does the output reach customers or anyone outside the organisation? If yes, it is middle tier. Otherwise, it is low tier. Two modifiers: a system that is generative or agentic is out of the guidance's scope, which changes the label on the evidence, not the tier; and a shared component, such as a vendor foundation model, takes the highest tier of any system that depends on it. The rule is the lesson's, not the guidance's; the guidance gives materiality, not tier names.

blocks.caption: Tiers and the controls each one carries (practice, not requirement)

rows.pick_when: The output decides or acts on money, people or legal standing without per-case human approval
rows.avoid_when: A person reviews every output before anything happens; demoting it hides the real exposure if the review is a rubber stamp
rows.example: Credit scorecard; payment-sending agent; the foundation model the agent runs on. Controls: inventory entry, validation before first use by an independent validator, effective challenge with standing to block, outcomes analysis on a fixed cadence, monitoring with alerting, vendor evidence and contingency, internal audit coverage

rows.pick_when: The output reaches customers or outsiders, but a person or a hard limit sits between the output and any irreversible action
rows.avoid_when: The chatbot can trigger refunds, cancellations or account changes on its own; that is high tier
rows.example: Retrieval chatbot answering customer questions. Controls: inventory entry, evaluation gate with graded samples before launch, challenge by someone outside the team, sampled outcomes grading in production, guardrails, every model or prompt change treated as a change event

rows.pick_when: The output is read by staff who make the decision themselves, and nothing outside the organisation sees it
rows.avoid_when: Staff paste the output into customer-facing or regulatory documents unchanged; then it is effectively middle or high
rows.example: LLM summariser for internal documents. Controls: inventory entry, pre-deployment test on a sample with pass criteria, confabulation monitoring on sampled output, version pinning, periodic review

rows.pick_when: Deterministic rules or arithmetic with no statistical method; excluded by the definition
rows.avoid_when: The rules were derived from a model's output or a threshold tuned on data; then it inherits the model's tier
rows.example: A fee table or a fixed routing rule. Controls: software change control and tests; an inventory line if a material decision depends on it

blocks.text: Write the tier rule down before you tier anything, and tier every system in the inventory with it, including the ones that look harmless. The guidance's own warning is that a sound model becomes high risk when misused; a summariser whose output is pasted into customer letters has changed tier without anyone changing the code.

worked_example.title: Tier five systems with the stated rule

blocks.text: An organisation runs the five systems below and wants one inventory with one tier rule. Apply the three questions and the two modifiers from the tiering subtopic to each, note whether the banking guidance applies as written or as practice, and recount at the end.

blocks.title: Classify each system
items: Credit-scoring scorecard. It applies statistical theory to produce a quantitative estimate, so it is a model, and the footnote names "traditional statistical and quantitative models" as in scope. Its score decides applications without per-case approval: high tier. Every principle applies as written: inventory, validation before first use, effective challenge, outcomes analysis by back-testing, monitoring, documentation, audit. Running count of high tier: 1.

LLM summarising documents for staff. Generative, so the footnote puts it out of the guidance's scope; the principles apply as practice. Staff read the summary and act themselves, and nothing leaves the organisation: low tier. Controls: inventory entry, a pre-deployment test on a sample with written pass criteria, sampled confabulation checks in production, a pinned model version. Running count of low tier: 1.

Retrieval chatbot answering customers. Generative, so the footnote puts it out of scope; practice. It does not act on accounts, but customers read it: middle tier. Controls: evaluation gate with graded samples, challenge from outside the team, guardrails, sampled grading of live conversations, change events for every prompt or model update; information integrity and confabulation from the profile's risk list in the validation plan. Running count of middle tier: 1.

Tool-using agent that can send payments. Agentic, out of scope, practice. It acts on money without a person approving each case: high tier. Controls: everything the scorecard gets, plus hard limits on amount and recipients, a human approval threshold, tool-call monitoring, and the "autonomous agents" line in the profile's security and resilience subcategory in the security evaluation. Running count of high tier: 2.

Vendor-hosted foundation model, used by the summariser, the chatbot and the agent. Section VII applies to vendor products, and the footnote still applies because it is generative. Weights and data are unavailable, so validation rests on the vendor's documentation and on testing of each use. Shared-component modifier: it takes the highest dependent tier, which is the agent's. Running count of high tier: 3.

Recount. Five systems: one in scope as written (the scorecard), four out of scope governed as practice. By tier: three high (scorecard, agent, foundation model), one middle (chatbot), one low (summariser). Three plus one plus one is five, which matches the inventory, so no system was dropped.

Sample test with pass criteria, confabulation checks, pinned version
Evaluation gate, challenge record, graded production samples, guardrail tests
Everything in the high tier plus limits, approval threshold, tool-call monitoring, security evaluation

blocks.text: The point of the recount is not arithmetic. It is that the inventory and the tier list must agree, because the inventory is what an auditor or a customer's risk team reads first, and a system that is in one list and not the other is the finding they write up.

What a validation report contains. The 2011 text is explicit: "Validation reports should articulate model aspects that were reviewed, highlighting potential deficiencies over a range of financial and economic conditions, and determining whether adjustments or other compensating controls are warranted", and effective reports "include clear executive summaries, with a statement of model purpose and an accessible synopsis of model and validation results, including major limitations and key assumptions". The revised guidance frames conceptual soundness as "assessing and documenting model design (including key modeling choices, assumptions, qualitative judgments, and data selection), construction, and developmental testing". For an LLM system the same outline works: purpose, the design and why (model, prompt, retrieval, tools), the test set and criteria, results, failure modes found, limitations, and the conditions under which use was approved.

Why vendor-model validation rests on documentation and testing. You cannot inspect what you do not receive, and the guidance accepts that a vendor may withhold "the underlying code, data, or methodology". What remains is the vendor's documentation (testing results, stated limitations and assumptions, the model's change history) and your own testing of your use. The 2011 text expected banks to "validate their own use of vendor products"; the profile's MANAGE 3.1 action lists filtering, grounding, fine-tuning and retrieval as the controls applied to third-party resources; the framework's GOVERN 6.2 asks for contingency processes for failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed high-risk. Put all three in the report: what the vendor says, what you tested, and what you do if the vendor changes the model.

Keeping the inventory current. The 2011 text wanted a firm-wide inventory covering models "implemented for use, under development for implementation, or recently retired", maintained by a named party; the revised text calls a comprehensive set of information for models "under development or in use" common industry practice; the AI RMF asks in GOVERN 1.6 for mechanisms to inventory AI systems and in GOVERN 1.7 for processes to decommission them safely, and the profile's first action under that subcategory wants protocols that ensure generative systems "are able to be deactivated when necessary". In engineering terms: register at design time, update status at every gate, record every model and prompt version change as an event, and keep retired entries so that a decision made last year can still be traced to the model that made it.

What the evidence is for. The 2011 text says documentation should be detailed enough that "parties unfamiliar with a model can understand how the model operates, its limitations, and its key assumptions", and names the readers: developers, users, control and compliance units, and supervisors. The revised text says documentation supports "the tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions", and that internal audit's role is generally to evaluate whether the model risk management practices themselves are rigorous and effective. So the evidence set for any system, in or out of scope, is the inventory entry, the validation report, the challenge record with each recommendation and its response, the exception list with approvals, the monitoring reports, and the change log. If a question about the system cannot be answered from those six documents, the gap is the finding.
